p.seg: A descendant of the Emperor Dì Gāoyáng,
my late father was called Bóyōng.
When the star Shètí was upright in the month of Mèngzōu,
on the day Gēngyín, I was born.
My father observed and measured my initial carriage,
and first bestowed on me a fine name.
He named me Zhèngzé,
and gave me the courtesy name Língjūn.
Abundant is the inner beauty I already possess,
and I have added to it cultivated talents.
Clad in river-selière and secluded angelica,
I weave autumn orchids to wear as a pendant.
Swiftly I move as if I cannot keep up,
fearing the years will not wait for me.
In the morning I pluck magnolias from Pí Shān,
in the evening I gather winter-grass from the islets.
Sun and moon hurry on without lingering,
spring and autumn follow each other in succession.
Thinking of how the trees and grass wither and fall,
I fear the Fair One will arrive at the twilight of life.
Why not take advantage of youth to cast off impurities?
Why not change these ways?
Mount the Qíjì steed and gallop forth;
come, I shall lead the way ahead!
Of old, the Sān Hòu were pure and perfect,
truly, they were where all fragrances gathered.
They mixed Shēnjiāo with Jùnguì;
did they only weave Huì and Chǎi?
Yáo and Shùn were brilliant and upright;
they followed the Way and found the path.
How wild and reckless were Jié and Zhòu;
they took shortcuts and stumbled in their steps.
Those factionalists seek only illicit pleasure;
their path is dark, treacherous, and narrow.
It is not that I fear personal calamity,
but I fear the royal carriage will be wrecked.
Hurrying to and fro, before and behind,
to follow in the footsteps of former kings.
Quán does not examine my inner feelings,
but instead believes slanders and flares up in anger.
I well know that forthright speech brings trouble,
yet I endure it and cannot give it up.
I point to the Nine Heavens to be my witness:
it is all for the sake of the Língxiū.
He appointed the dusk as our trysting time,
but alas, halfway he changed his course.
At first he gave me his solemn word,
but later he regretted it and turned elsewhere.
It is not that I find parting difficult,
but I am grieved by the Língxiū's frequent changes.
I have already nurtured nine wǎn of orchids,
and planted a hundred mǔ of Huì.
I laid out plots of Liúyí and Jiēchē,
mixed with Dùhéng and fragrant Zhǐ.
Hoping their branches and leaves would grow tall and lush,
wishing to wait for the time when I might harvest them.
Though they wither and die, what is the harm?
I grieve that the many flowers have turned to weeds.
The crowds all scramble to advance with greed,
unsatisfied in their incessant seeking.
They pardon themselves and measure others,
each harboring malice and envy.
Suddenly they gallop in pursuit,
but these are not the things my heart desires.
Old age is gradually approaching,
I fear my cultivated name will not be established.
In the morning I drink the fallen dew of magnolias,
in the evening I eat the fallen petals of autumn chrysanthemums.
If my feelings are truly beautiful and refined,
what harm is there in being forever haggard?
I grasp tree roots to bind the Chǎi,
and thread the fallen blossoms of the Ficus.
I straighten Jùnguì to weave with Huì,
and twist the strands of Húshéng into long cords.
Truly, I model myself after the cultivated ones of old,
not what the common world wears.
Though I do not fit in with the people of today,
I wish to follow the legacy of Péng Xián.
Long do I sigh and wipe away my tears,
grieving for the many hardships of the people's lives.
Though I love cultivation and beauty, I am restrained;
in the morning I am rebuked, and in the evening I am dismissed.
I was dismissed because I wore a sash of Huì,
and further accused because I gathered Chǎi.
Yet this is what my heart finds good;
though I die nine deaths, I shall have no regrets.
I resent the Língxiū's lack of restraint,
who never examines the hearts of the people.
The many women envy my moth-like eyebrows,
and spread slanders, calling me wanton.
Truly, the artisans of this age's customs
disregard the compass and square to change their measures.
They turn from the marking line to follow crookedness,
competing to see who can be most agreeable.
Grieved and dejected, I am lost and forlorn;
I alone am destitute in this age.
I would rather die suddenly and vanish
than endure to act in such a manner.
Birds of prey do not flock together;
it has been so since ancient times.
How can a square and a circle fit together?
Who can follow different paths and still be at peace?
I humble my heart and suppress my will,
enduring blame and bearing insults.
To maintain purity and die for uprightness
was what the former sages highly prized.
I regret not having examined the path more carefully;
I pause and linger, for I shall turn back.
I turn my carriage to return to the path
before I have strayed too far.
I walk my horse along the orchid-covered bank,
galloping to the Pepper Hill to take my rest.
Advancing, I could not enter and so met with blame;
retiring, I shall return to cultivate my original attire.
I make a tunic of water-chestnut and lotus leaves,
and gather hibiscus flowers for my skirt.
If no one knows me, so be it,
so long as my inner feelings are truly fragrant.
I make my cap even taller,
I make my pendants even longer and more dazzling.
Fragrance and brilliance are mixed together;
only my bright quality remains undiminished.
Suddenly I look back and let my eyes roam,
going to observe the four wildernesses.
My pendants are colorful and many-ornamented;
their scent is rich and more manifest.
Every living person has their own joy;
I alone love cultivation as my constant rule.
Though my body be dismembered, I shall not change;
how could my heart be deterred by punishment?
Nǚ Xū was anxious and concerned;
again and again she scolded me.
She said: "Gǔn was stubborn and upright, losing his life,
ending up dead on the wilds of Yǔ Shān.
Why are you so outspoken and fond of cultivation,
standing alone with such beautiful integrity?
Cockleburs, green-grass, and weeds fill the room,
yet you alone stay apart and will not wear them.
One cannot go from door to door to explain to the crowds;
who will observe your inner feelings?
The world moves in groups and loves factions;
why remain isolated and not listen to me?"
I followed the former sages to find the middle way;
sighing, I followed my heart to this point.
I crossed the Yuán and Xiāng rivers to journey south,
to approach Chónghuá and lay out my words:
Qǐ performed the Jiǔbiàn and the Jiǔgē,
the Xià house indulged in pleasure and self-abandon.
Not considering hardships or planning for the future,
so the five brothers lost their family home.
Yì wandered excessively and lived for the hunt,
and loved to shoot the giant foxes.
Truly, a life of chaos seldom has a good end;
Zhuó, in turn, coveted Yì's wife.
Jiāo was physically strong and powerful,
he indulged his desires without restraint.
Daily seeking pleasure and forgetting himself,
so his head fell and he perished.
Jié of Xià constantly violated the right path,
and so he finally met with calamity.
The Sovereign Xīn minced and salted his subjects,
so the Yīn dynasty did not last long.
Tāng and Yǔ were solemn and reverent;
the Zhōu kings discussed the Way without error.
They promoted the worthy and employed the capable,
following the marking line without bias.
August Heaven has no favorites;
it observes people's virtue and grants support accordingly.
Only the wise and sagely with excellent conduct
can thus be granted the rule of this earth below.
Looking to the past and observing the future,
I contemplate the ultimate plans for the people.
Who that is not righteous can be of use?
What that is not good can be followed?
I have endangered myself and risk death,
yet looking back at my beginning, I still have no regrets.
To shape the tenon without measuring the mortise,
indeed, the cultivated ones of old were minced and salted for this.
Sobbing and sighing in my dejection,
I grieve that my time is out of joint.
I take soft Huì to wipe away my tears,
wetting my lapel with their streaming flow.
I kneel on my outspread robe to present my plea;
clearly, I have attained this inner balance.
Harnessing four jade hornless dragons to a phoenix carriage,
suddenly, amidst dust and wind, I journey upward.
In the morning I set out from Cāngwú,
by evening I reach the Xiánpǔ gardens.
I wish to linger a while at this sacred gate,
but the sun is hurrying toward the twilight.
I command Xīhé to slow the pace,
to gaze at Mount Yānzī and not press near.
The road is long and stretches far away;
I shall search high and low.
I water my horses at the Xiánchí pool,
I tie my reins to the Fúsāng tree.
I break a branch of the Ruòmù tree to brush against the sun,
wandering and roaming for a while.
I bid Wàngshū to be my precursor,
I bid Fēilián to follow behind.
The Luánhuáng birds clear the way before me,
Léishī tells me the preparations are not yet complete.
I order the Fèng bird to soar high,
continuing day and night.
Whirlwinds gather and then disperse,
leading clouds and rainbows to welcome me.
They crowd together, parting and meeting,
in multicolored splendor rising and falling.
I command the Dìhūn to open the gates,
he leans against the Chānghé and gazes at me.
The day grows dim and draws to a close,
I knot the secluded orchid and stand waiting long.
The world is turbid and knows no distinctions,
it delights in hiding beauty out of jealousy.
In the morning, I will cross the Báishuǐ,
climb the Làngfēng peaks and tether my horse.
Suddenly I look back and shed tears,
grieving that on the high hill there is no lady.
Suddenly I travel to this Chūngōng,
I break off a jade branch to add to my pendants.
While the blossoms have not yet fallen,
I seek a maiden below to whom I may give it.
I order Fēnglóng to mount the clouds,
to search for where Fúfēi dwells.
I unfasten my sash to pledge my word,
I order Jiǎnxiū to act as my go-between.
Many are the partings and meetings,
suddenly she is wayward and hard to move.
In the evening, she returns to stay at Qióngshí,
in the morning, she washes her hair in the Wěipán.
Guarding her beauty with arrogance,
daily she abandons herself to pleasure.
Although truly beautiful, she lacks propriety,
so I turn away and seek elsewhere.
I gaze and look to the four poles,
traveling all through the heavens, I descend.
I see the Yáotái tower soaring high,
and see the beautiful lady of Yǒusōng.
I order the Zhèn bird to be my matchmaker,
but the Zhèn bird tells me she is not good.
The male dove flies off cooing,
yet I dislike its flighty craftiness.
My heart wavers in doubt,
I wish to go myself, but it is not possible.
The Fènghuáng has already received the gifts,
I fear Gāoxīn has preceded me.
I wish to alight far away but have no place to rest,
so I drift and roam for a while.
While Shǎokāng is not yet married,
the two Yáo maidens of Yǒuyú remain.
My messenger is weak and the matchmaker clumsy,
I fear the message will not be firm.
The world is turbid and jealous of the worthy,
delighting in hiding beauty and praising evil.
The inner chambers are deep and distant,
the wise king does not awaken.
I harbor my feelings but cannot voice them,
how can I endure this forever?
I seek the Qióngmáo grass and bamboo splints,
and bid Língfēn to divine for me.
He says: “Two beauties must surely match;
who truly cultivates himself and is not admired?”
“Think of the vastness of the Jiǔzhōu;
is it only here that there are ladies?”
He says: “Strive to go far away and do not doubt;
who seeking beauty would pass you by?”
“Where is there not fragrant grass?
Why do you cling to your old home?”
The world is dark and dazzlingly confused,
who can discern my good or evil?
People’s likes and dislikes differ,
but this faction is uniquely strange.
Every household fills its waist with mugwort,
and says that secluded orchids cannot be worn.
They look at plants and trees but still do not understand,
how could they appreciate the beauty of Chéng jade?
They fill their bags with dung and soil,
and say the Shēnjiāo is not fragrant.
I wish to follow Língfēn’s auspicious divination,
but my heart wavers in doubt.
Wū Xián will descend in the evening,
I will carry pepper and fine rice to welcome him.
A hundred gods darken the sky as they descend,
from Jiǔyí they come in a throng to meet him.
The August One radiantly reveals his spirit,
telling me of auspicious things.
He says: “Strive to ascend and descend, to go up and down,
seeking those who share the same measure.”
“Tāng and Yǔ were reverent and sought matches,
Zhì and Jiùyáo could harmonize with them.”
“If one’s inner heart truly loves cultivation,
why must one use a matchmaker?”
“Yuè worked with a building-ram at Fùyán,
Wǔdīng employed him without doubt.”
“Lǚ Wàng wielded the butcher’s knife,
he met Zhōu Wén and was raised up.”
“Nìng Qī sang his songs,
Qí Huán heard him and made him an assistant.”
“While the years are not yet late,
and the time has not yet come to an end.”
“I fear the shrike will sing too soon,
making all the grasses lose their fragrance.”
How magnificent are the jade pendants!
The crowd obscures them in darkness.
This faction is not faithful,
I fear they will break them out of jealousy.
The times are chaotic and changing,
how can I linger here?
The orchids and angelicas change and lose fragrance,
the Quán and Huì turn into rank grass.
Why have the fragrant grasses of former days
now become merely mugwort and wormwood?
Is there any other reason?
It is the fault of not loving cultivation.
I thought the orchid was to be relied upon,
but alas, it has no substance, though its appearance is fair.
It abandons its beauty to follow the crowd,
content to be ranked among ordinary flowers.
The pepper is sycophantic and arrogant,
the dogwood also wants to fill the perfume bag.
Since they strive only for advancement,
how can they maintain any fragrance?
Indeed, they follow the flow of the times,
who then can avoid changing?
Seeing that pepper and orchid are like this,
what then of the Jiēchē and Jiānglí?
Only my jade pendant is precious,
its beauty remains through all this.
Its fragrance is rich and hard to diminish,
its scent even now has not faded.
I harmonize my bearing to amuse myself,
and roam about to seek a lady.
While my adornments are still in their prime,
I travel all around, looking above and below.
Língfēn has given me an auspicious divination,
I choose a lucky day to set out.
I break a jade branch for my food,
and grind fine jade for my provisions.
Harness flying dragons for me,
a chariot of jasper and ivory.
How can divergent hearts be united?
I will go far away and distance myself.
I direct my path toward Kūnlún,
the road is long and far as I wander.
Raising the cloud-banners into the gloom,
the jade phoenix-bells tinkle softly.
In the morning, I set out from Tiānjīn,
in the evening, I reach the western limit.
Phoenixes hover, supporting my banners,
soaring high in orderly flight.
Suddenly I cross these Liúshā,
I follow the Chìshuǐ and linger there.
I beckon the water-dragons to bridge the ford,
I command the Xīhuáng to ferry me across.
The road is long and full of hardships,
I send the many chariots ahead to wait at the crossroads.
Passing Bùzhōu, I turn left,
pointing toward the Xīhǎi as my goal.
I gather my chariots by the thousands,
lining up their jade hubs to gallop together.
Harnessing eight dragons that writhe and wind,
carrying cloud-banners that stream and coil.
I check my will and slow my pace,
my spirit soars high into the distance.
I play the Jiǔgē and dance the Sháo,
taking advantage of the time to steal a moment of joy.
Ascending to the brilliant light of heaven,
suddenly I look down and see my old home.
My groom is sad and my horses yearn,
they curl back, looking around and refusing to go.
Envoi:
It is all over!
There are no people in the country, no one knows me,
why should I still cling to the old capital?
Since there is no one with whom I can manage good government,
I will go to follow the dwelling place of Péng Xián.
2.1 Dōnghuáng Tàiyī
On this auspicious day and at this lucky hour,
solemnly I will please the High Sovereign.
Grasping the long sword by its jade hilt,
the jade pendants tinkle and chime.
Jasper mats and jade weights,
why not take up the jade-like blossoms?
Offerings of Huì meat on orchid mats,
libations of cassia wine and pepper broth.
Raising the drumsticks and beating the drums...
Relax the rhythm and sing peacefully,
Set out the reed-organs and zithers in grand chorus.
The spirit moves gracefully in beautiful robes,
Fragrance overflows, filling the hall.
The five notes mingle in complex harmony;
My Lord is joyful, happy, and at ease.
2.2 *Yún Zhōng Jūn*
Bathed in orchid water and washed in fragrances,
Wearing colorful robes like blossoming flowers.
The spirit, coiling and curling, has stayed;
Brilliant and radiant without end.
Grandly about to rest in the *Shòu Gōng*,
Equal in light with the sun and moon.
Riding a dragon carriage in imperial robes,
For a moment soaring and wandering about.
The spirit, majestic and bright, has descended;
Swiftly it rises far into the clouds.
Surveying *Jì Zhōu* and far beyond,
Spanning across the four seas, where could it end?
Thinking of my Lord, I sigh deeply;
My heart is utterly troubled and anxious.
2.3 *Xiāng Jūn*
You do not come, Lord, but hesitate;
Alas, for whom do you linger on the mid-stream isle?
Beautiful and delicate, refined and well-adorned;
Swiftly I ride my cassia boat.
I command the *Yuán* and the *Xiāng* to be without waves,
Make the waters of the *Jiāng* flow peacefully!
I look for my Lord, but he does not come;
I play the panpipes, thinking of whom?
Driving flying dragons, I journey north,
Turning my path toward *Dòng Tíng*.
Ivy and cypress form the curtains of orchid,
Angelica for oars and orchids for banners.
Gazing toward the distant shores of *Cén Yáng*,
Crossing the Great *Jiāng*, I manifest my spirit.
Manifesting my spirit, but not yet reaching the goal;
The ladies are sorrowful and sigh for me.
My tears flow down in streams;
Secretly longing for you, I am pained and distressed.
Cassia oars and orchid sweeps,
Carving through ice and accumulated snow.
Picking ivy in the water;
Plucking lotus from the treetops.
Hearts not in accord make the matchmaker's toil in vain;
Affection that is not deep is easily severed.
The rocky shallows flow babbling,
The flying dragons soar gracefully.
Infidelity in friendship leads to long resentment;
You broke your promise and told me you were busy!
In the morning I race along the *Jiāng* banks,
In the evening I halt my pace at the northern islet.
Birds roost upon the roof,
Water encircles below the hall.
I cast my jade ring into the *Jiāng*,
I leave my pendant at *Lǐ Pǔ*.
Gathering fragrant pollia on the flowery isle,
To give to the maiden below.
Time cannot be regained;
For a while I wander and take my ease.
2.4 *Xiāng Fū Rén*
The Emperor's daughter descends to the northern islet;
Her eyes gaze into the distance, making me sad.
Gently blows the autumn wind;
Waves rise on *Dòng Tíng*, and the leaves fall from the trees.
Among the white reeds I gaze afar,
Meeting with the fair one at the evening's appointed time.
Birds gather in the duckweed;
Why is the fishing net upon the tree?
The *Yuán* has its angelica, the *Lǐ* has its orchids;
I think of the prince but dare not speak.
In a daze, I look into the distance,
Watching the flowing waters ripple along.
Why do the elk eat in the courtyard?
Why does the dragon linger at the water's edge?
In the morning I gallop my horse along the *Jiāng* banks,
In the evening I cross to the western shore.
Hearing that the fair one has summoned me,
I will mount my carriage and go with her.
I will build a house in the midst of the water,
Thatched with a roof of lotus leaves.
Walls of angelica and an altar of purple,
Scattering fragrant pepper to make a hall.
Cassia for beams and orchids for rafters,
Magnolia for lintels and angelica for the chamber.
Weaving ivy to make the curtains,
Splitting sweet-grass for the screens already set.
White jade for weights,
Scattering rock-orchids for fragrance.
Angelica thatching the lotus roof,
Wreathed with pollia.
Gathering a hundred herbs to fill the courtyard,
Establishing a sweet scent at the porch and gate.
The spirits of *Jiǔ Yí* come in a throng to welcome her;
The spirits arrive like clouds.
I cast my sleeve into the *Jiāng*,
I leave my undershirt at *Lǐ Pǔ*.
Picking pollia on the sandy isle,
To give to one who is far away.
Time cannot be easily regained;
For a while I wander and take my ease.
2.5 *Dà Sī Mìng*
Wide open are the gates of Heaven,
In a throng, I ride upon the dark clouds.
I command the whirlwind to be my herald,
Make the rainstorm wash away the dust.
You hover and soar as you descend,
Crossing over *Kōng Sāng* to follow me.
Teeming are the people of the Nine Provinces,
How longevity or early death lies with me!
Flying high, soaring peacefully,
Riding the pure air, I master Yin and Yang.
You and I, Lord, in solemn haste,
Guide the Sovereign to the Nine Peaks.
My spiritual robes are flowing,
My jade pendants are glittering.
Now Yin, now Yang,
None among the crowd knows what I do.
I pluck the blossoms of the sacred hemp,
To give to the one who dwells apart.
Old age has gradually reached its limit,
Not drawing closer, but becoming ever more distant.
Riding a dragon with a clatter,
Soaring high into the sky.
Binding cassia branches, I linger long,
Alas, the more I think, the more I grieve.
What can be done about this grief?
I wish that now there would be no loss.
Human life has its destined end,
Who can control meeting and parting?
2.6 *Shǎo Sī Mìng*
Autumn orchids and clover,
Grow in rows below the hall.
Green leaves and white stalks,
Fragrance overflows and envelops me.
People naturally have beautiful children,
Why, Lord, are you so full of sorrow?
Autumn orchids are verdant,
Green leaves and purple stems.
The hall is full of beautiful people,
Suddenly, with me alone, eyes have met.
Entering without a word, leaving without a farewell,
Riding the whirlwind, carrying cloud banners.
No sorrow is greater than the parting of the living,
No joy is greater than newly making an acquaintance.
Robes of lotus and a belt of sweet-grass,
Suddenly you come and suddenly you vanish.
In the evening you lodge in the Sovereign's suburbs,
For whom, Lord, do you wait at the edge of the clouds?
I wander with you by the Nine Rivers,
A sudden wind arrives and the water raises waves.
I bathe with you in *Xián Chí*,
I dry your hair at the slope of the Sun.
I look for the fair one, but she does not come;
Facing the wind, I am dazed and sing a grand song.
Canopy of peacock feathers and banners of kingfisher,
Ascending to the Nine Heavens to touch the Comet.
Grasping a long sword, I protect the young and the fair;
You, *Sūn*, alone are fit to be a judge for the people.
2.7 *Dōng Jūn*
The bright sun is about to emerge in the East,
Shining upon my railing from *Fú Sāng*.
I pat my horse and drive peacefully;
The night was bright, and now it is dawn.
Driving a dragon chariot, riding the thunder,
Carrying cloud banners that trail behind.
I sigh deeply as I am about to ascend;
My heart lingers, looking back with longing.
Sounds and sights surely please people,
The spectators are content and forget to return.
Tighten the zither strings and beat the drums,
Strike the bells on the jade stands.
Sound the flutes and blow the reed organs,
Thinking of the shaman, talented and beautiful.
Soaring like birds in a kingfisher dance,
Reciting poems and joining in the dance.
In tune with the rhythm and keeping the beat;
The arrival of the spirit obscures the sun.
Robes of blue clouds and skirts of white rainbow,
Lifting a long arrow to shoot the *Tiān Láng*.
Grasping my bow, I return and descend,
Taking up the Northern Dipper to pour cassia wine.
Holding my reins, I soar high,
Into the dark depths, I journey eastward.
2.8 *Hé Bó*
I wander with you by the Nine Rivers,
A sudden wind rises, and cross-waves surge.
Riding a water chariot with a lotus canopy,
Drawn by two dragons and flanked by hornless dragons.
I climb *Kūnlún* and gaze in the four directions,
My heart soars, grand and expansive.
The sun is about to set, and I am sad, forgetting to return;
Thinking only of the distant shore, I wake with longing.
Fish-scale roofs and dragon halls,
purple shell gateways and vermilion palaces.
Why does the spirit dwell in the water,
riding a white soft-shell turtle and chasing patterned fish?
Wandering with you on the river's islet;
the drifting ice swirls as the current flows down.
Hand in hand with you, we travel east,
seeing the fair one off at the southern shore.
The billowing waves come to welcome us;
the fish in shoals escort me.
2.9 Shān Guǐ
There seems to be someone in the mountain's fold,
clad in creeping fig and girdled with dodder.
With a sidelong glance and a lovely smile,
you admire me for my graceful charm.
Riding a red leopard, followed by a striped civet;
a chariot of magnolia with banners of cinnamon.
Clad in rock orchids and girdled with wild ginger,
I pluck fragrant blossoms to give to the one I love.
I dwell in a dark bamboo grove where the sky is never seen;
the road is steep and difficult, so I arrive alone and late.
I stand alone atop the mountain;
the clouds billow and roll below.
All is dark and misty, even the day is dim;
the east wind blows and the spirits send down rain.
Waiting for the noble one, I linger and forget to return;
the year is late—who will make me bloom?
Gathering the divine herb among the mountains,
where rocks lie heaped and creepers grow tangled.
Resenting the young lord, I sadly forget to return;
you think of me, but have no leisure to come.
The person of the mountain is fragrant as pollia;
drinking from stone springs, shaded by pines and cypresses.
You think of me, yet doubts arise.
The thunder rumbles and the rain falls dark;
the monkeys chatter and cry through the night.
The wind soughs and the leaves rustle;
thinking of the young lord, I suffer grief in vain.
2.10 Guó Shāng
Grasping spears of Wú and wearing rhinoceros-hide armor,
chariot hubs clash and short blades meet.
Banners blot out the sun, the enemy is like clouds;
arrows fall in crossfire as soldiers strive to be first.
Breaking our ranks and trampling our lines, breaking our ranks and trampling our lines,
the left trace-horse falls dead, the right one is wounded by a blade.
Two wheels are buried, the four horses are tied;
grasping the jade drumsticks, I beat the sounding drum.
Heaven's time fails and the mighty spirits are angry;
the grim slaughter is complete, the bodies abandoned on the wild plains.
They went out never to return, departed never to come back;
the plain is vast and the way is far.
Wearing long swords and carrying bows of Qín;
though head and body are severed, the heart knows no regret.
Truly brave and truly martial,
steadfast to the end and never to be cowed.
Though the body dies, the spirit is divine;
your souls shall be heroes among the ghosts.
2.11 Lǐ Hún
The ritual is complete to the beating of drums;
passing the flower-sprig, dancers take their turns.
Lovely maidens sing with slow and easy grace;
spring orchids and autumn chrysanthemums.
May they never cease for all eternity.
It is said:
At the very beginning of remote antiquity,
who was there to pass down the story?
Before the high and the low had taken shape,
by what means could they be examined?
When darkness and light were confused and dim,
who could determine their ultimate source?
In the vast and swirling chaos,
how could anyone recognize its form?
Light became bright and darkness became deep;
what caused this to happen at that time?
The Yīn and Yáng and the Three joined together;
what was their origin and how did they transform?
The celestial sphere has nine layers;
who designed and measured them?
Whose great work was this?
Who first created it?
Where is the cord of the axis fastened?
Where is the celestial pole attached?
Where do the eight pillars stand?
Why is the southeast deficient?
Where the nine heavens meet,
how are they placed and joined?
There are many corners and bends;
who knows their number?
Where does the heaven join the earth?
How are the twelve signs divided?
How are the sun and moon attached?
How are the stars arrayed?
Emerging from Tānggǔ
and resting in Méngsì.
From dawn until dusk,
how many miles do they travel?
What virtue does the moon have,
to die and then be reborn?
What benefit is there
for it to keep a hare in its belly?
Nǚqí had no husband;
how did she obtain nine sons?
Where does Bóqiáng dwell?
Where is the auspicious wind?
What closing makes it dark?
What opening makes it light?
Before the Horn constellation rises in the dawn,
where is the brilliant spirit hidden?
Since he was not equal to the task of controlling the flood,
why did the people recommend him?
They all said, "What worry is there?
Why not test him and let him proceed?"
The owl and turtle dragged and carried;
why did Gǔn heed them?
He followed his desires to achieve success;
why did the Emperor punish him?
Forever imprisoned on Yǔshān,
why was he not released for three years?
Bóyǔ was born from Gǔn;
how did the father undergo such a transformation?
He took up his father's unfinished work
and brought the task to success.
Why, in continuing the original task,
was his plan different?
The flood waters were extremely deep;
how did he fill them in?
The earth was divided into nine regions;
how did he bank them up?
The Winged Dragon and the river and sea,
where did it complete its markings and where did it pass?
What did Gǔn plan?
What did Yǔ achieve?
Kānghuí was filled with rage;
why did the earth tilt toward the southeast?
How were the Nine Provinces arranged?
Why are the river valleys hollowed out?
They flow east without overflowing;
who knows the reason why?
East, west, south, and north—
which dimension is the longer?
From south to north it is an elongated oval;
what is its extent?
The Hanging Gardens of Kūnlún,
where is their location?
The layered walls are ninefold high;
how many miles is their height?
Through the gates of the four directions,
who passes through?
When the northwest gate is opened,
what wind passes through there?
Where does the sun not reach?
Where does Zhúlóng shine?
Before Xīhé has set forth,
how can the Ruòhuá flowers shine?
In what place is it warm in winter?
In what place is it cold in summer?
Where is there a stone forest?
What beast can speak?
Where is there a horned dragon
that carries a bear on its back as it wanders?
The male serpent with nine heads,
darting about—where is it?
Where is the place of immortality?
What do the giants guard?
The water-shield has nine branching stems;
where do the hemp flowers dwell?
A snake swallows an elephant;
how large must it be?
Hēishuǐ and Xuánzhǐ,
where is Sānwēi located?
One prolongs life and does not die;
where does such longevity end?
Where is the scaly fish-man?
Where does the Qíduī dwell?
How did Yì shoot down the suns?
How did the crows shed their feathers?
Yǔ exerted his strength to achieve great deeds,
descending to inspect the four quarters of the earth.
How did he find that girl of Túshān
and mate with her at Táisāng?
He joined with his consort in marriage,
that his lineage might continue.
Why did they have different tastes in food,
yet satisfy themselves with a single morning's meal?
Qǐ replaced Yì as the sovereign,
and suddenly encountered misfortune.
Why was Qǐ so full of anxiety,
yet able to escape from restraint?
They all returned to their archery and hunting, and no harm came to his person.
Why did Sovereign Yì make changes,
and why did Yǔ's descendants decline?
Qǐ was an urgent guest of the Supreme God,
obtaining the Jiǔ Biàn and the Jiǔ Gē.
Why did the diligent son cause his mother to be split open,
so that at her death her body was divided upon the ground?
The Lord sent down Yí Yì,
to reform the calamities of the Xià people.
Why did he shoot Hé Bó,
and take Luò Pín as his wife?
With his jade-adorned bow and sharp thumb-ring,
he shot the giant boar.
Why was the fat of the sacrificial meat offered,
and yet the High Lord did not approve?
Zhuó married Chún Hú,
and the seductive wife conspired with him.
Why did Yì's archery fail him,
and they conspired together to swallow him up?
Blocked at the western limits of the journey,
how did he cross the cliffs?
Having transformed into a yellow bear,
how did the shamans revive him?
They all sowed black millet,
and cultivated the reeds and rushes.
For what reason were they cast out together,
while Gǔn's legacy of error continued to grow?
White rainbows encircled the sash;
why was this hall built?
Where did he obtain the elixir of immortality,
yet could not keep it safe?
Heaven’s laws run both vertical and horizontal;
when the Yáng leaves, one then dies.
Why did the great bird cry out,
and how did it lose its body?
Píng called out and the rain rose;
how did he stir it?
With a coiled body and joined ribs,
how did the deer receive it?
The giant turtles bear the mountains on their heads and clap their flippers;
how are they kept steady?
Leaving the boat to travel by land,
how did they move it?
When Āo was at the door,
what did he seek from his sister-in-law?
Why did Shǎo Kāng use hunting dogs,
and cause his head to fall?
Nǚ Qí was sewing a garment,
and they stayed together in the same house;
why was the wrong head cut off,
and he met his end through his own kin?
Tāng planned to rearrange the troops;
how did he strengthen them?
Overturning the boats at Zhēn Xún,
by what path was it taken?
Jié attacked Méng Shān;
what did he gain there?
Why was Mò Xǐ so willful,
and why did Tāng execute him?
Shùn was distressed at home;
why did his father leave him without a wife?
Yáo did not inform Shùn's father;
how could the two daughters become his wives?
When the sprout first appeared,
how could its future be foretold?
The Jade Tower had ten stories;
who reached its peak?
Ascending to be established as Emperor,
whose Way was esteemed?
Nǚ Wā had a body;
who fashioned and created her?
Shùn yielded to his brother,
yet in the end, he was harmed.
Why did he behave like a wild dog,
and yet his person was not ruined?
Wú flourished until ancient times,
stopping at Nán Yuè.
Who expected to leave this place,
and obtain two sons?
Trimming the swan and decorating with jade,
the High Lord enjoyed the offering.
Why did he help plot against Xià Jié,
to bring about his final destruction?
The Lord then looked down,
and met Yī Zhì below.
Why was the punishment at Tiáo Shān carried out,
and the common people were greatly pleased?
Jiǎn Dí was on the tower; how was Kù a suitable match?
The Dark Bird brought a gift; why was the maiden glad?
Gāi upheld the virtue of Jì,
and his father was praised.
Why was he finally ruined at Yǒu Hù,
while herding the oxen and sheep?
Holding the shields and dancing in rhythm,
how were they comforted?
With flat ribs and smooth skin,
how was he made so stout?
The shepherd lad of Yǒu Hù,
how did he meet him?
Hitting the bed and escaping first,
where did his fate lead?
Héng upheld the virtue of Jì;
how did he obtain those sturdy oxen?
Why did he go to seek rewards,
and did not just return?
Hūn Wēi followed the trail,
making the Yǒu Dí people uneasy.
Why did the many birds gather on the thorns,
bearing the child and following their whims?
The seductive brother joined in the debauchery,
and brought harm to his elder brother.
Why did he use transformations to deceive,
yet his descendants prospered for so long?
Chéng Tāng traveled to the East,
and reached Yǒu Shēn.
Why did he ask for that lowly servant,
and obtain a lucky bride?
From the tree by the water's edge,
that young child was found;
why was he disliked,
and sent as a dowry-servant for the Yǒu Shēn woman?
Tāng came out of Zhòng Quán;
what crime or fault did he have?
Unable to restrain his heart, he attacked the Sovereign;
who provoked him to do so?
Meeting at dawn to vie for the alliance,
how did they keep the appointed time?
The dark birds flew in flocks;
who made them gather?
Striking at the person of Zhòu,
Shū Dàn did not approve.
Why did he personally guide Fā
to fully
fulfill the Mandate of Zhōu with sighs?
Having granted the world to Yīn,
where was the position established?
Success was reversed into ruin;
what was the sin?
Contending to send out the weapons of war,
how were they deployed?
Driving together to strike the flanks,
how were they led?
King Zhāo completed his journey,
and reached the southern lands.
What was the gain,
to encounter that white pheasant?
King Mù was clever and ambitious;
why did he travel all around?
Making his circuit to order the world,
what did he seek?
The strange man hawked his wares;
why did he cry out in the market?
Whom did Zhōu Yōu execute,
to obtain Bāo Sì?
The Mandate of Heaven is fickle;
whom does it punish, and whom does it favor?
Qí Huán convened nine assemblies,
yet in the end his body was left to perish.
As for the person of King Zhòu,
who caused him to be so deluded?
Why did he hate his ministers,
and trust only the slanderers?
How did Bǐ Gān rebel,
to be suppressed and destroyed?
Léi Kāi was fawning and obedient;
why was he granted a fief?
Why do sages share the same virtue, yet in the end their ends are so different?
Méi Bó was minced into meat;
Jī Zǐ feigned madness.
Jì was the eldest son;
why did the Lord treat him harshly?
He was cast upon the ice;
why did the birds keep him warm?
Why, grasping his bow and clutching his arrows,
was he so uniquely able to lead?
Having startled the Lord and provoked Him,
why did he prosper for so long?
Bó Chāng lamented the decline,
holding the whip to serve as a shepherd.
Why did he order the removal of the altar at Qí,
and receive the mandate over the land of Yīn?
Moving his treasures to Qí,
how could they rely on it?
Yīn had a deluded woman;
what was there to mock?
Having been given the gift of this minced meat,
Bó Chāng reported to Heaven.
Why did he personally receive the High Lord's punishment,
so that the Mandate of Yīn could not be saved?
Shī Wàng was in the market;
how did Bó Chāng recognize him?
Rattling his knife and raising his voice,
why was the King so pleased?
Wǔ Fā slew the King of Yīn;
what was there to be sorrowful about?
Carrying the corpse to the battle,
why such haste?
Bó Lín hung himself;
for what reason?
Why were Heaven and Earth so moved,
and whom did they fear?
August Heaven bestowed the Mandate;
what was the warning?
Having received the world through ritual,
why was another brought to replace him?
At first Zhì was a minister of Tāng,
and later Cí served as an assistant.
Why did Tāng finally execute an official
yet honor the sacrifices of his ancestral line?
If merit is hidden and life is like a dream,
separated and wandering since youth.
Why was his martial power so fierce
that he could spread his majesty?
Péng Kēng offered pheasant stew;
why did the Emperor enjoy it?
He received a long life and many years;
why did it last so long?
All were shepherds in the center;
why was the Lord angry?
Bees and moths have tiny lives;
why is their strength so firm?
The startled girl gathering vetch;
why did the deer bless her?
Reaching north to the circling waters;
what was the joy of the gathering?
The elder brother had a biting dog;
what did the younger brother want?
Exchanging it for a hundred carriages,
in the end, he had no fortune.
In the evening dusk, thunder and lightning,
what was the worry in returning?
If his majesty is not upheld,
what does the Emperor seek?
Hiding and dwelling in a cave,
what was said then?
Jīng's merit raised an army;
how could it last long?
Realizing the error and changing;
what more can I say?
Wú Guāng fought for the state;
for a long time, I have been victorious.
Why does the ring pass through from the village gate to the mounds,
and from there Zǐ Wén emerged?
I told Dǔ Áo that he would not last long.
Why did he test his superior and give of himself,
so that his loyal name became even more manifest?
4.1 Xī Sòng
I lament my words to express my grief,
and release my indignation to pour out my feelings.
I act with loyalty and speak of it,
pointing to the blue heaven as my witness.
I ask the Wǔ Dì to judge the middle,
and caution the Liù Shén to listen and submit.
Let the mountains and rivers be prepared to testify,
and command Gāo Yáo to hear the truth.
Exhausting my loyalty and sincerity to serve the lord,
yet instead, I am cast out like a useless growth.
Forgetting flattery and turning against the crowd,
I wait for a wise lord to understand.
My words and deeds can be traced;
my feelings and appearance do not change.
Thus, no one knows a minister like the lord,
so the evidence is not far off.
My duty is first to the lord and then to myself,
which is why the common people hate me.
I focus only on the lord and no other,
which is why the masses treat me as an enemy.
With a single heart and no hesitation,
yet I cannot be protected.
Bitterly close to the lord and no other,
this is a way to invite disaster.
Thinking that no one is more loyal to the lord than I,
I suddenly forget my own lowliness and poverty.
Serving the lord without double-mindedness,
I am lost and do not know the gates of favor.
For what crime is loyalty punished?
This was not the intent of my heart.
My actions do not follow the crowd and I fall,
and the masses laugh at me.
Often meeting with blame and suffering slander,
I cannot be released.
My feelings are suppressed and not conveyed,
and they are obscured so none can be made clear.
My heart is depressed and I am distraught,
yet no one perceives my inner feelings.
Truly, many words cannot bind a promise,
and I wish to express my will but have no path.
Withdrawing in silence, no one knows me;
coming forward to cry out, no one hears me.
I repeat my distraught confusion,
my heart troubled and dazed.
Formerly I dreamed of climbing to heaven,
but my soul had no boat in mid-passage.
I asked the Lì Shén to divine it,
and he said I had reached the limit of my will but had no companion.
In the end, I am perilously alone and separated;
he said the lord may be longed for but not relied upon.
Therefore, many mouths can melt gold;
at the start, it was like this and I met with danger.
One who has been scalded by soup blows on cold leeks;
why do I not change this will?
Wanting to leave the stairs and climb to heaven,
I still have the same attitude as before.
The masses are shocked and their hearts are estranged;
why should I take them as companions?
Going to the same limit but by different paths;
why should I take them as my support?
Jìn Shēn Shēng was a filial son,
but his father believed slander and did not love him.
Gǔn acted with stubborn uprightness and did not hesitate,
but his work was not completed.
I heard that acting with loyalty creates resentment,
and I suddenly thought it was an exaggeration.
Breaking one's arm nine times makes one a doctor;
I know now that it is truly so.
Arrows and traps are above,
and nets are spread below.
They set traps to please the lord;
I wish to hide but have nowhere to go.
I want to wander and find relief,
but I fear repeated trouble and meeting with blame.
I want to fly high and settle far away,
but the lord would ask where I am going.
I want to run wildly and lose my way,
but my firm will cannot endure it.
My back and chest are split with mutual pain;
my heart is knotted and twisted with grief.
Pounding Mù Lán to improve the Huì,
and grinding Shēn Jiāo for food.
Sowing Jiāng Lí and growing Jū;
I hope for the spring days to make them fragrant.
Fearing that my inner nature is not trusted,
I repeatedly write to explain myself.
Restraining this charm to live in seclusion,
I wish to think more and distance myself.
4.2 Shè Jiāng
In my youth, I loved this unusual dress,
and even in old age, it does not fade.
I wear a long sword of many colors,
and a high Qiè Yún cap.
Wearing Míng Yuè pearls and precious Lù jade.
The world is turbid and no one knows me,
so I gallop high and do not look back.
Driving a blue Qiú dragon and yoking a white Chī dragon,
I travel with Chóng Huá in the Yáo garden.
Climbing Kūnlún to eat the jade blossoms,
living as long as heaven and earth,
and shining with the same light as the sun and moon.
Mourning that the southern barbarians do not know me,
at dawn I cross the Jiāng and Xiāng.
Passing È Zhǔ and looking back,
I sigh at the lingering winds of autumn and winter.
I walk my horse on the mountain banks,
and rest my carriage in Fāng Lín.
Boarding a small boat to go up the Yuán,
hitting the waves with rhythmic oars.
The boat drifts and does not move,
lingering in the circling waters and hesitating.
At dawn leaving Wǎng Zhǔ,
at evening staying in Chén Yáng.
If only my heart is upright and straight,
what does it matter if I am in a remote place?
Entering Xù Pǔ, I wander about,
lost and not knowing where to go.
The deep forest is dark and dim,
the dwelling place of apes and monkeys.
The mountains are steep and high, blocking the sun;
below it is dark and murky with much rain.
Sleet and snow fall endlessly,
and the clouds are thick and touch the eaves.
Mourning that my life has no joy,
I live alone in the mountains.
I cannot change my heart and follow the crowd,
so I will surely end in sorrow and poverty.
Jiē Yú shaved his head,
Sāng Hù walked naked.
Loyalty is not necessarily used,
and virtue is not necessarily employed.
Wǔ Zǐ met with calamity,
Bǐ Gān was minced and salted.
It was the same in former generations,
so why should I complain about the people of today?
I will follow the path and not hesitate,
even if I must remain in darkness for the rest of my life!
Envoi:
The Luán bird and the Fèng Huáng fly further away every day.
Swallows, sparrows, crows, and magpies nest in the halls and altars.
Lù Shēn and Xīn Yí die in the thickets.
Foul and rank things are used together, so fragrance cannot come near.
Yīn and Yáng have changed places; the time is not right.
Holding my faith and feeling distraught,
suddenly I shall depart!
4.3 Āi Yǐng
August Heaven is not constant in its mandate;
why must the common people suffer such shock and error?
The people are scattered and lose one another,
as in mid-spring we migrate to the east.
Leaving the old home to go far away,
following the Jiāng and Xià rivers into exile.
Passing through the city gates with a heavy heart,
on the morning of the day Jiǎ I set out.
Departing Yǐng Dū and leaving its neighborhoods,
in confusion, where will I find rest?
The oars rise together as the boat moves slowly;
I grieve that I shall not see my Lord again.
Looking at the tall catalpas, I heave a deep sigh;
my tears flow endlessly like sleet.
Passing Xià Shǒu and floating to the west,
I look back for Lóng Mén but see it no more.
My heart is tied in knots and filled with sorrow;
gazing into the distance, I know not where I tread.
Following the wind and waves, drifting with the current;
a wanderer on the vast waters.
Riding the swelling waves of Yáng Hóu;
drifting aimlessly, where will I stop?
My heart is tangled and cannot be unknotted;
my thoughts are twisted and cannot be released.
I turn the boat to float downstream,
up to Dòng Tíng and down to the Jiāng.
Leaving the place where I lived since of old;
now I wander and come to the east.
Oh, how my soul longs to return;
not for a moment do I forget to go back.
Turning my back on Xià Pǔ and thinking of the west;
I grieve as the old capital grows more distant by the day.
Climbing Dà Fén to look afar;
for a while I soothe my troubled heart.
I grieve for the peace and joy of the land;
I mourn for the old customs of the Jiāng region.
When I reach Líng Yáng, where did I arrive?
Where will I go, crossing the waters to the south?
Little did I know that Xià would become a mound;
who would have thought the two East Gates would be overgrown with weeds?
My heart has not been at ease for a long time;
worry and sorrow follow one another.
I contemplate the long road to Yǐng;
the Jiāng and Xià rivers cannot be crossed.
It seems suddenly unbelievable;
nine years have passed, and I have not returned.
Miserable and dejected, my path is blocked;
in distress and disappointment, I harbor grief!
Outwardly, they show graceful and charming faces;
but truly they are weak and hard to rely on.
My loyalty is profound and I wish to step forward;
but a crowd of jealous people blocks the way.
The lofty conduct of Yáo and Shùn
was so high it reached the distant heavens.
The jealousy of the slandering crowd
covers them with the false name of being unfilial.
They hate the cultivation of inner beauty;
they prefer those who are boastful and arrogant.
The crowd scurries forward day by day;
but the beautiful and virtuous are pushed far away.
Envoi:
I cast my eyes around to gaze widely,
hoping for a time when I might once return.
Even a bird flies back to its old home;
even a dying fox turns its head toward its native mound.
Truly I was discarded and banished through no fault of my own;
how could I forget this day or night?
4.4 Chōu Sī
My heart is filled with gloomy and worried thoughts;
alone I sigh forever in increasing pain.
My thoughts are twisted and cannot be released;
I have encountered a night that is just beginning to be long.
I grieve as the autumn wind changes its expression;
why are the cycles of the universe so vast and shifting?
Constantly I think of how the Sūn is often angry;
it wounds my heart with sorrow.
I wish to rise up and run across the land;
but I look at the people's errors to steady myself.
Gathering my hidden feelings to express in words;
I present them to that Beautiful One.
Long ago, you and I spoke sincerely;
you said dusk would be the time for our meeting.
But alas, you turned back halfway and betrayed me;
you have turned around and had these other intentions.
You pride yourself on your own beauty;
you show me your refined elegance.
You spoke to me but were not truthful;
you surely were manufacturing anger against me.
I wish to wait for a quiet moment to explain myself;
but my heart trembles with fear and I dare not;
I am grieved and hesitant, yet hope to proceed;
my heart is pained and restless.
I lay out my feelings to express in words;
but the Sūn pretends to be deaf and does not hear.
Truly, an honest person is not pleasing to others;
the crowd indeed considers me a nuisance.
What I stated at the beginning was bright and clear;
could it be that it has vanished by now?
Why is the medicine of blunt words so bitter?
I only wish that the beauty of the Sūn could be kept whole.
I look to the Sān Wǔ as my models;
I point to Péng Xián as my example.
What goal is there that cannot be reached?
Thus, a reputation heard afar is hard to diminish.
Goodness does not come from the outside;
a name cannot be made falsely.
Who can receive a reward without giving anything?
Who can have a harvest without planting seeds?
Lesser Song:
I draw out my resentment toward the Beautiful One;
day and night there is no justice.
He prides himself on his beauty;
he treats my words with disdain and will not listen.
Prelude:
There is a bird from the south;
it has come to settle north of the Hàn River.
It is lovely and beautiful;
but it lives alone and separated in this foreign land.
Since it is lonely and has no companions;
and there is no good matchmaker at its side.
The road is far and it is forgotten day by day;
it wishes to express itself but cannot.
Looking at the northern mountains, I shed tears;
standing by the flowing water, I heave deep sighs!
Looking at the short nights of Mèng Xià;
why does the time from dark to light seem like a whole year!
I contemplate the long road to Yǐng;
my soul departs nine times in a single night.
I do not know if the road is winding or straight;
looking south at the moon and the stars.
I wish to go directly but cannot;
my soul knows the road and is restless.
Why is my soul so honest and direct?
The hearts of others are not like mine!
My influence is weak and no matchmaker conveys my message;
they still do not know my calm and composed nature.
Envoi:
The long shallows and the rushing torrents, I sail up the Jiāng's deep pools.
Looking back wildly as I go south, for a while I amuse my heart.
The jagged rocks are high and rugged, my wishes are frustrated.
I cross over my former will and change my plans, my journey is hidden and slow.
Hesitating and lingering, I lodge at Běi Gū.
My face is troubled and confused; truly I have gone to the wetlands.
Worried and sighing, my spirit is bitter; my soul wanders in distant thoughts.
The road is far and the place is secluded; and there is no matchmaker to go for me.
I compose a song of my road and thoughts, for a while to save myself.
My troubled heart finds no fulfillment; to whom shall I tell these words?
4.5 Huái Shā
In the swelling waters of Mèng Xià;
the plants and trees grow lushly.
With a wounded heart and eternal grief;
I go swiftly to the southern lands.
Gazing into the vast and distant;
all is silent and secluded.
My heart is tied in knots and filled with anguish;
I suffer from neglect and long confinement.
Examining my feelings and testing my will;
I am wronged and suppressed.
They carve a square to make it round;
but the constant measure has not been discarded.
Changing one's original path;
is what a gentleman finds despicable.
I clearly mark the plan and follow the ink-line;
the former pattern has not been changed.
Inwardly thick and of upright quality;
this is what a great person values.
If Qiǎo Chuí does not carve;
who will see the correction of the flaws?
Dark patterns in a secluded place;
the blind say they are not bright.
When Lí Lóu looks with a slight gaze;
the sightless think there is no light.
They change white to black;
and turn the top into the bottom.
The phoenix is in a cage;
while chickens and ducks fly and dance.
They mix jade and stones together;
measuring them by the same standard.
Only those of the petty clique are mean and stubborn;
they surely do not know what I possess.
Bearing a heavy burden and carrying much;
I am stuck and cannot cross over.
Embracing the jǐn-jade and holding the yú-jade;
in my distress, I know not to whom to show them.
The village dogs bark in a pack;
they bark at what they find strange.
To slander the talented and doubt the heroic;
is indeed the way of the mediocre.
Refinement and substance are scattered within,
yet the masses know not my extraordinary brilliance.
Raw timber is piled and heaped,
yet none know what I possess.
Doubling benevolence and layering righteousness,
I take careful sincerity as my wealth.
Chónghuá cannot be encountered;
who knows my composed bearing?
From of old, things have not always coexisted;
how can one know the reason why?
Tāng and Yǔ are long distant;
remote, they cannot be followed.
Chastened by sorrow and checking my anger,
I suppress my heart and strengthen myself.
Suffering misery without shifting,
I wish my will to have an image.
Advancing on the road and resting in the north,
the sun is dim and about to set.
Soothing worry and entertaining grief,
I limit them by the Great Event.
*Luàn* says:
The vast Yuán and Xiāng rivers flow apart, surging along.
The long road is dark and hidden, the way distant and blurred.
Carrying substance and embracing emotion, I alone have no match.
Bólè having passed away, how can the Jì-steed be judged?
The lives of the myriad people each have their place.
With a settled heart and broad will, what should I fear?
Repeatedly pained and grieving here, I sigh and lament forever.
The world is turbid and knows me not;
the human heart cannot be spoken to.
Knowing that death cannot be avoided,
I wish not to cherish life.
Clearly I tell the gentlemen:
I shall take them as my kind.
4.6 *Sī Měirén*
Thinking of the beauty,
I wipe away tears and gaze afar.
The matchmaker is cut off and the road blocked;
words cannot be joined and sent.
The frustration and resentment of being upright
is trapped and stagnant, unable to break forth.
Morning after morning I express my inner feelings,
but my will is depressed and pent up, unable to reach through.
I wish to send my words upon the floating clouds,
but I meet Fénglóng who will not lead them.
Relying on the returning birds to deliver my message,
alas, they roost high and are hard to reach.
Gāoxīn’s spirit was grand and flourishing;
he encountered the Xuánniǎo and sent his gift.
I wish to change my principles to follow the custom,
but I am ashamed to alter my original intent and bend my will.
Alone I have spent years suffering distress,
yet my stubborn heart remains unchanged.
Better to hide in misery and live a long life;
what change or alteration could I commit!
Knowing the former tracks do not succeed,
I still have not changed this measure.
The carriage is overturned and the horses toppled,
yet I stubbornly hold to this different path.
I rein in the Qíjì and harness them again;
let Zàofù drive them for me.
Advancing slowly and stopping in turn without rushing,
I briefly borrow time to wait for the moment.
Pointing toward the western corner of Bāzhǒng,
I set a tryst with the sunset's crimson and yellow light.
The new spring begins the year;
the bright sun comes out in its leisure.
I shall let my will wander and find pleasure,
following the Jiāng and Xià rivers to entertain my worries.
I gather the fragrant Chǎi from the thickets,
and pluck the evergreen Sùmǎng from the long isle.
I regret I cannot reach the ancients;
with whom shall I enjoy these fragrant herbs?
Gathering the Biān-thickets and mixed greens,
I prepare them to be joined as a pendant.
The pendants are numerous and swirling,
but then they wither and fall away.
I shall wander about to entertain my worries
and observe the changing ways of the southern people.
Secretly finding pleasure in my heart,
I give vent to my pent-up feelings and do not wait.
Fragrance and luster are mixed together,
yet the fragrant flower naturally emerges from within.
Its dense fragrance reaches far,
full within and manifesting without.
Feeling and substance can truly be preserved;
though living in concealment, one’s fame is brilliant.
I would have the fig-creeper act as a go-between,
but I dread lifting my feet to climb the tree.
I would rely on the lotus to be a matchmaker,
but I dread tucking up my skirt and wetting my feet.
Climbing high I do not enjoy,
going down low I cannot do.
Truly my form does not comply,
so I hesitate and waiver.
I broadly follow my previous plan,
and have not changed this measure.
If fate means staying in darkness, I shall be exhausted;
I wish to reach the time before the bright sun sets.
Alone and solitary I travel south,
thinking of the old ways of Péng Xián.
4.7 *Xī Wǎng Rì*
I lament that in the past I was once trusted,
and received orders and decrees to clarify the poems.
Carrying on the ancestors' achievements to illuminate those below,
I clarified the laws and regulations and settled doubts.
The state was rich and strong, and the laws were established;
it was entrusted to upright ministers, and daily we rejoiced.
Secret matters were carried in the heart;
even if there were faults, they were not yet punished.
The heart was pure and simple without leaking secrets,
but then I encountered slanderers who were jealous of me.
The Lord harbored anger and waited for his minister,
without clarifying what was true or false.
They obscured the Lord's intelligence,
with empty delusions, errors, and further deception.
He did not investigate or examine the facts,
but banished his minister far away without thought.
He believed the turbidity of slander and flattery,
full of arrogance and passing over the truth.
How is it that an upright minister is without guilt,
yet suffers slander and is blamed?
Ashamed of the sincerity of the sun and moon,
I keep myself in darkness and prepare for the end.
Facing the deep abyss of the Yuán and Xiāng,
I then steel myself and sink into the current.
Finally ending my life and cutting off my name,
I regret that the obstructed Lord is not enlightened.
The Lord lacks measure and does not observe,
making the fragrant herbs dwell in the dark marshes.
How can I express my feelings and draw out my sincerity?
I am at peace with death and do not wish to live.
Alone I am blocked and hidden away,
leaving the upright minister with no way forward.
I heard that Bǎilǐ was a captive,
and Yī Yǐn cooked in a kitchen.
Lǚ Wàng was a butcher in Zhàogē,
and Nìng Qī sang while feeding oxen.
Had they not met Tāng, Wǔ, Huán, and Mù,
who in the world would have known them?
Wú believed slander and did not appreciate the truth;
Zǐxū died, and only then did sorrow follow.
Jièzǐ was loyal and died standing withered,
Wén Jūn awoke and pursued him.
He enfeoffed Jiè Shān and made it a forbidden area,
to repay the great virtue with leisure.
Thinking of the long-standing bond with his person,
he donned white hemp and wept for him.
Some are loyal and faithful and die for their principles;
others are deceitful and arrogant without being doubted.
He does not examine or check the facts,
but listens to the empty words of slanderers.
Fragrance and luster are mixed together;
who will distinguish them morning after morning?
Why do the fragrant herbs die so early?
A slight frost falls and warns those below.
Truly his hearing is not sharp and his sight is obscured,
allowing slanderers and flatterers to succeed daily.
Since ancient times they have been jealous of the worthy,
saying that the Huì and Ruò cannot be worn.
Envious of the fragrance of the beautiful,
Mómǔ is called lovely and admires herself.
Even if there is the beauty of Xī Shī,
slander and envy enter to take her place.
I wish to state my feelings to clarify my conduct,
but I met with unexpected guilt and faults.
My grievances are seen more clearly each day,
like the stars arranged in the sky.
Riding the Qíjì and galloping along,
without reins or bit, one is carried along;
riding a raft down the stream,
without oars or rudders, one prepares oneself.
Turning one's back on the laws and governing by the heart,
the error is no different from this.
Better to die suddenly and drift away,
for I fear calamities will occur again.
Without finishing my words, I rush into the abyss,
regretting that the obstructed Lord does not understand.
4.8 *Jú Sòng*
O auspicious tree of Hòuhuáng, the orange has come to be acclimated.
Receiving its mandate not to move, it grows in the southern lands.
Deep-rooted and hard to transplant, it has a single-minded purpose.
Green leaves and white blossoms, so lush and delightful.
Thick branches and sharp thorns, the round fruits are well-formed.
Green and yellow are mixed together, the patterns are brilliant.
Pure of color and white within, its kind is worthy of trust.
Flourishing and well-fitted, beautiful and not ugly.
Ah, your youthful will has something different!
Standing alone and not shifting, is that not delightful?
Deep-rooted and hard to transplant, expansive and without seeking.
Independent in a world of turmoil, standing firm and not drifting with the current.
I close my heart and practice self-caution, that I may never fall into error or fault.
Holding to virtue without selfishness, I am a peer to Heaven and Earth.
I wish that as the years pass away together, I may remain your lifelong friend.
Pure and detached without excess, upright and possessed of inner principle.
Though young in years, you are fit to be a teacher and elder.
In conduct you are the equal of Bó Yí; I set you up as my model.
4.9 Lament for the Eddying Wind
I grieve for the eddying wind that shakes the Huì orchids,
My heart is knotted with resentment and I am wounded within.
Some things are so frail that they lose their nature,
Some sounds are so faint that they lead the chorus.
Why does the thought of Péng Xián arise in my mind,
To be joined with a steadfast will that cannot forget!
How can the myriad changes of emotion be hidden?
How can falsehood and hypocrisy endure?
Birds and beasts cry out to call their kind,
Dried grass and weeds huddle together, lacking fragrance.
Fish arrange their scales to distinguish themselves,
Dragons hide their brilliant patterns.
Thus, bitter herbs and sweet shepherd’s purse grow not in the same field,
Lán and Chǎi orchids dwell in seclusion, alone in their fragrance.
Only the fair one is forever beautiful,
Passing through successive generations, bestowing grace upon themselves.
Remote is the reach of my far-aiming will,
I pity the floating clouds as they wander to and fro.
My steadfast, distant will is troubled by doubt,
I secretly compose poems to make my feelings clear.
Only the fair one cherishes such solitary thoughts,
Plucking Ruò flowers and Jiāo peppers to dwell in purity.
Ever sighing with deep sobs,
Dwelling in seclusion, lost in contemplation.
Tears and weeping mingle in bitter grief,
Thinking so deeply I cannot sleep until the dawn.
Throughout the long night that stretches on and on,
I harbor this sorrow and it does not leave.
Awaking, I wander calmly and travel about,
Briefly roaming free to sustain myself.
I sigh with pain and pity for myself,
My breath is choked with distress and cannot be stopped.
I twist my yearning thoughts into a sash,
And weave my sorrows into a breastplate.
I break a branch from the Ruò tree to shield the light,
Following where the whirling wind leads.
A faint image remains but cannot be seen,
My heart leaps and seethes like boiling water.
I touch my jade pendants and robes to steady my will,
Journeying on in a daze across the void.
The years pass swiftly as if tumbling down,
Time creeps slowly on and is about to arrive.
The Fán and Héng plants wither and their joints part,
Their fragrance has faded and they are no longer matched.
I pity my yearning heart that cannot be restrained,
I bear witness that these words offer no comfort.
I would rather pass into death and drift away,
Than endure this constant state of sorrow.
An orphan wails and wipes away tears,
An exile goes out and does not return.
Who can think on this without secret pain?
I look to what was heard of Péng Xián.
I climb the rocky peaks to gaze afar,
The road is distant, vast, and silent.
I enter the realm of shadows and echoes where there is no response,
I listen for a sound, but find nothing.
My sorrow is heavy and provides no joy,
Dwelling in distress that cannot be dispelled.
My heart is bridled and tethered, yet formless,
My spirit winds and twists, knotting itself.
Solemn and vast without limit,
Desolate and boundless without form.
Sounds are faint yet stir each other,
Things are pure yet cannot be feigned.
Distant and spreading, beyond measure,
Misty and continuous, not to be unraveled.
Quiet is my sorrow, a constant grief,
Flitting in the darkness, there is no pleasure.
Riding the great waves and the flowing wind,
I entrust myself to the dwelling place of Péng Xián.
Climbing the steep banks of high cliffs,
I stand upon the very tip of the secondary rainbow.
Resting on the blue void, I stretch out the rainbow,
Suddenly and swiftly I touch the sky.
I drink from the floating source of clear dew,
I rinse my mouth with the falling thick frost.
I rest myself by the cavern of the winds,
Suddenly I wake and feel a deep attachment.
Resting on Kūnlún, I look down upon the mist,
Sheltering by Mín Shān to clear the Jiāng.
I dread the thundering of the surging rapids,
I listen to the roaring of the waves.
In chaotic confusion without order,
In boundless vacancy without a trace.
Pressing through the vast expanse without a path,
Galloping along winding ways, where will I stop?
Drifting and fluttering up and down,
Soaring far to the left and right.
Floating and surging in front and behind,
Following the certain cycle of expansion and contraction.
I watch the fiery vapors following one another,
I peer at where the misty fluids accumulate.
I grieve for the frost and snow falling together,
I listen to the tide-waters striking each other.
I borrow the light and shadow to come and go,
Applying the crooked switch of yellow thorns.
I seek where Jiè Zǐ dwells,
And see the traces of Bó Yí in his exile.
My heart is set and will not leave them,
My will is engraved and has nowhere else to go.
I say:
I resent what I hoped for in the past,
I mourn the anxiety of what is to come.
Floating on the Jiāng and Huái to enter the sea,
I follow Zǐ Xū and find my own peace.
Gazing at the islands and sandbars of the Great River,
I grieve for the noble traces of Shēn Tú.
Repeatedly he admonished his lord, who would not listen,
What was the use of jumping into the river with a heavy stone?
My heart is snagged and knotted, and will not be undone,
My thoughts are tangled and will not be released.
I grieve for the narrowness of the current age,
I wish to rise lightly and roam afar.
My substance is meager and I have no means,
How can I find a carriage to float upwards?
Meeting with the sunken, turbid, and defiled,
Alone and frustrated, to whom can I speak?
Restless through the night, I cannot sleep,
My soul is solitary until the dawn.
Only Heaven and Earth are infinite,
I lament the long labor of human life.
I cannot reach those who have gone before,
I do not hear of those yet to come.
I pace to and fro, thinking of distant things,
Despondent and distracted, my heart is ill at ease.
My mind is blurred and drifting,
My heart is sorrowful and my grief increases.
My spirit has suddenly departed and does not return,
My body is withered and remains alone.
Internally I examine myself to rectify my conduct,
Seeking the source of the righteous Qi.
In the vastness of void and stillness, I find peace and joy,
Tranquil in non-action, I find myself.
Hearing of the pure dust of Chì Sōng,
I wish to follow the wind of his legacy.
I value the excellent virtue of the True Man,
I admire those of past ages who ascended to immortality.
Passing away with the transformation, they are seen no more,
Their fame is manifest and spreads daily.
Marveling at Fù Yuè who entrusted himself to Chén Xīng,
Envying Hán Zhòng who attained the One.
Their forms were solemn and grew ever more distant,
Leaving the world of men and escaping into seclusion.
Following the transformation of Qi, they rose high,
Suddenly their spirits raced off in marvelous ways.
Sometimes appearing faintly in the distance,
Their bright spirits coming and going.
They cast off the dust of the world and became transcendent,
Never returning to their old capitals.
Free from all troubles and without fear,
No one in the world knows where they have gone.
I fear the succession of the seasons,
The Bright Spirit shines as it journeys westward.
Faint frost falls and sinks below,
I mourn the fragrant herbs that wither first.
For a while I wander and roam free,
Though years have passed and I have achieved nothing.
With whom can I enjoy this lingering fragrance?
In the morning, I face the wind and pour out my feelings.
Gāo Yáng is remote and far away,
Where shall I find my path?
Envoi:
Spring and Autumn pass quickly and do not stay,
Why remain long in this old dwelling?
Xuān Yuán cannot be reached,
I shall follow Wáng Qiáo in joyful play!
I shall eat the Six Qi and drink the midnight dew,
Rinse my mouth with the midday sun and breathe the morning glow.
I shall preserve the clarity of my spirit,
Pure Qi shall enter and coarse defilement be removed.
Following the south wind to roam,
Reaching Nán Cháo to take a rest.
I meet the Wáng Zǐ and stay with him,
To examine the harmonious virtue of the One Qi.
He says:
"The Dào can be received,
but not transmitted;
its smallness has no interior,
its greatness has no limit;
Do not disturb your soul,
and it will be natural;
when the One Qi is most spiritual,
it remains within in the deep of night.
Wait for it with emptiness,
do not precede it with action.
Thus all things are completed;
this is the gate of virtue.
Hearing of the most precious, I then departed;
suddenly I am about to go.
I follow the Feathered Men to Dān Qiū,
and stay in the old home of immortality.
In the morning, I wash my hair in Tāng Gǔ;
in the evening, I dry my body in the Nine Suns.
I sip the subtle fluid of the flying springs,
and harbor the flowery brilliance of wǎnyǎn jade.
My complexion is ruddy and my face is glowing,
my essence is pure and I begin to grow strong.
My physical form melts away and becomes delicate,
my spirit becomes ethereal and roams freely.
I praise the flaming virtue of the Southern State,
and the beauty of the cassia trees blossoming in winter.
The mountains are desolate and without beasts,
the wilds are lonely and without people.
Carrying my soul, I ascend to the clouds,
brushing past the floating mists to journey upward.
I command the Gatekeeper of Heaven to open the gate,
he pushes open the Chānghé Gate and gazes at me.
I summon Féng Lóng to lead the way,
and ask for the dwelling place of Tàiwēi.
I gather the layered yang to enter the Emperor's Palace,
reach Xúnshǐ and view the Qīngdū.
In the morning, I set out from Tàiyí,
in the evening, I first arrive at Wēilǘ.
I gather my chariot of ten thousand horses,
in a bustling throng they gallop together.
I harness eight dragons that wind gracefully,
and carry cloud banners that trail behind.
I set up the colorful plumes of the great rainbow,
their five colors mixed and dazzling.
The team of horses bends and rises,
the side horses curl and leap with pride.
The riders are a tangled and chaotic mass,
speckled and spreading as they advance.
I grasp my reins and adjust my whip,
I am about to pass by Gùmáng.
Passing Tàihào, I turn to the right,
with Fēi Lián ahead to clear the path.
The sun shines brightly but has not yet peaked,
I traverse heaven and earth in a direct crossing.
Fēng Bó serves as my vanguard,
sweeping away dust to make it cool and clear.
Phoenixes flank me, supporting the banners,
I meet Rù Shōu at the Western Sovereign.
I seize a comet to use as a banner,
and lift the handle of the Dipper to use as a signal.
We dart up and down in brilliant confusion,
roaming through the flowing waves of startling mist.
The time is dark and vast,
I summon Xuán Wǔ to come and join.
I make Wén Chāng follow and manage the procession,
selecting and appointing the many gods to drive side-by-side.
The road is boundless and far-reaching,
I slowly slacken my pace and soar high.
On the left, I have Yǔ Shī wait in attendance,
on the right, Léi Gōng serves as my guard.
I wish to transcend the world and forget to return,
my mind is unrestrained and soaring.
Inwardly joyful and pleased with myself,
I briefly seek pleasure and amuse myself.
I wade through blue clouds in a broad roaming,
then suddenly I look down upon my old home.
My driver is homesick and my heart is sad,
the side horses look back and refuse to go.
Thinking of old friends with longing,
I sigh deeply and wipe away my tears.
Aimlessly wandering and soaring afar,
I briefly suppress my will and calm myself.
I point toward the God of Flame and gallop straight ahead,
I am going toward the Southern Yí.
I view the vast haze beyond the world,
floating freely in the formless void.
Zhù Róng warns me to return the yoke,
then sends a message for the luan bird to welcome Mì Fēi.
They strike up Xiánchí and play Chéngyún,
the two maidens perform the Jiǔsháo songs.
I have the Spirit of the Xiāng play the zither,
and order Hǎi Ruò to dance with Féng Yí.
Black dragons and sea monsters emerge together,
their forms writhing and undulating.
Rainbows are graceful and twisting,
luan birds soar and hover in the air.
The music spreads wide without end,
then I depart and wander to and fro.
I loosen the reins and gallop on,
reaching the far-off Hánmén.
Outstripping the swift wind at the Pure Source,
I follow Zhuānxū across the layered ice.
Passing through Xuánmíng by a side path,
I cross the space between the pillars and look back.
I summon Qián Yíng to see him,
to clear the level road ahead for me.
Traversing the four wildernesses,
roaming through the six voids.
Above reaching the Lièquē,
below looking toward the Great Abyss.
Below is steep and without ground,
above is vast and without heaven.
I look into the flickering void and see nothing,
I listen to the silence and hear nothing.
I transcend non-action to reach the ultimate purity,
and become a neighbor to the Great Beginning.
Qū Yuán had been banished; for three years he could not see the king again.
He had exhausted his wisdom and given his full loyalty,
yet he was obscured and blocked by slander.
His mind was troubled and his thoughts in turmoil,
not knowing which path to follow.
He went to see the Great Diviner Zhèng Zhānyǐn and said:
"I have some doubts,
and I wish for you, sir, to resolve them."
Zhānyǐn then straightened the stalks and brushed the tortoise shell,
saying: "What do you have to instruct me on?"
Qū Yuán said:
"Should I be sincere and earnest,
simple and loyal?
Or should I serve the social rounds without end?
Should I clear away weeds
and labor in farming?
Or should I roam among great men
to make a name for myself?
Should I speak directly without taboos
at the risk of my life?
Or should I follow the customs for wealth and honor
to live a stolen life?
Should I soar high and transcend everything
to preserve my truth?
Or should I be obsequious and fawning,
whispering and flattering
to serve women?
Should I be incorruptible and upright
to keep myself pure?
Or should I be slippery and artful,
like grease or leather,
to keep myself smooth?
Should I be proud like a thousand-mile steed?
Or should I float like a duck on the water,
rising and falling with the waves,
to stealthily preserve my body?
Should I share the yoke with the Qíjì horse?
Or should I follow in the tracks of a common nag?
Should I fly wing to wing with the yellow swan?
Or should I compete for food with chickens and ducks?
Which of these is auspicious and which is ominous?
What should I leave and what should I follow?"
"The world is turbid and not pure;
a cicada's wing is considered heavy,
and a thousand-jūn weight is considered light.
The yellow bell is broken and discarded,
while earthen pots thunder like drums.
Slanderers are in high positions,
while worthy men are nameless.
Alas, I remain silent;
who knows of my integrity and purity!"
Zhānyǐn then set down the stalks and excused himself, saying:
"A foot may be short,
an inch may be long;
things may be insufficient,
wisdom may be unclear;
numbers may not reach,
and spirits may not communicate.
Use your own heart,
and follow your own intent.
Tortoise shells and stalks truly cannot know this matter."
When Qū Yuán had been banished, he wandered by the river's edge,
walking and chanting on the banks of the marsh.
His complexion was withered,
and his form was gaunt.
A fisherman saw him and asked:
"Are you not the Sānlǘ Dàfū?
Why have you come to this?"
Qū Yuán said:
"The whole world is turbid and I alone am pure;
everyone is drunk and I alone am sober;
therefore I was banished."
The fisherman said:
"The Sage is not stuck in things,
but can change with the world.
If the people of the world are all turbid,
why not churn up the mud and splash the waves?
If everyone is drunk,
why not eat the dregs and drink the thin wine?
Why should you think so deeply and soar so high,
only to bring banishment upon yourself?"
Qū Yuán said:
"I have heard it said:
he who has newly washed his hair must flick his cap,
and he who has newly bathed must shake his robe.
How can one, with a body of such purity,
receive the foulness of worldly things?
I would rather plunge into the flow of the Xiāng,
to be buried in the bellies of the river fish.
How can I, with such brilliant whiteness,
be covered by the dust of the mundane world?"
The fisherman smiled faintly,
beat his oar, and went away.
He sang:
"When the waters of the Cāng Láng are clear,
they can wash my hat-strings;
when the waters of the Cāng Láng are muddy,
they can wash my feet."
Then he departed and did not speak with him again.
How sorrowful is the air of autumn!
Desolate—
the plants and trees shake, shed their leaves, and wither;
distressing—
as if one were on a long journey,
climbing mountains and looking over the water
to see off someone who is returning.
Vast and empty—
the sky is high and the air is clear;
silent and lonely—
