the puddles are dried up and the waters are still.
Grief and bitterness increase with sighs—
the slight cold strikes a person;
despondent and forlorn—
leaving the old to approach the new.
Thwarted and disappointed—
the poor scholar loses his position and his will is unsettled;
desolate and empty—
a traveler without companions.
Melancholy—
and privately pitying oneself.
Swallows flutter as they take their leave and return,
and the cicadas are silent, making no sound.
Wild geese flock together and travel south,
and the Kūn Jī birds chirp in mournful cries.
Alone until dawn without sleeping—
grieving for the night-traveling crickets.
Time passes busily beyond its peak,
yet I linger on, having achieved nothing!
Sorrowful, worried, and distressed, I dwell alone in the vastness;
there is a beautiful person whose heart is not at ease.
Leaving the village and departing home to become a distant traveler,
wandering far away—where do I rest now?
I single-mindedly think of the lord and cannot change,
but the lord does not know—what can be done!
Accumulating resentment and piling up thoughts,
the heart is troubled and I forget to eat.
I wish for one meeting to speak my mind,
but the lord's heart is different from mine.
The carriage is already harnessed and I return in haste,
but not being able to see him, my heart is wounded with grief.
I lean against the carriage-side and sigh deeply,
tears flow down like water, wetting the crossbar.
My fervent spirit is cut short and unfulfilled,
my mind is dazed and confused.
To what end shall my private self-pity go?
My heart beats with sincerity and uprightness.
August Heaven divides the four seasons equally,
yet I alone secretly grieve for this chilling autumn.
The white dew has already fallen upon the many grasses,
suddenly causing the Wú and Qiū trees to wither and droop.
Leaving the brilliance of the bright sun,
I enter the long, unending night.
Departing from the fragrant flowers in their prime,
I am withered and spent, filled with sorrow.
Since autumn first warned with white dew,
winter follows with harsh frost.
Withdrawing the vast warmth of early summer,
I am dejected and hidden away.
Leaves turn dark and lose their color,
branches are tangled and crisscrossed;
my countenance is faded and soon to fail,
the stems are faint and turn a withered yellow.
The thin and scattered foliage is piteous,
my form is wasted and bruised.
Thinking of the chaotic falling of leaves,
I regret missing the season and finding no place.
I take up the reins and slow my pace,
wandering about for a while.
The year passes hurriedly to its end,
and I fear my life will not last.
Mourning that my life was ill-timed,
I encounter this world of turmoil.
Calm and composed, I lean alone,
while the crickets chirp in this western hall.
The heart is fearful and shaken,
how varied are the things to worry about!
I look up at the bright moon and sigh deeply,
pacing among the stars until the height of light.
I secretly grieve that the Huì flowers once bloomed,
filling the capital's chambers with their grace.
Why did those flowers bear no fruit,
but were blown away by the wind and rain?
I thought you alone would wear this Huì,
but alas, you are no different from the common crowd of flowers.
Grieving that my extraordinary thoughts cannot be conveyed,
I shall leave you and soar high.
The heart is pained and wretched with sorrow,
wishing for one meeting to have clarity.
I loathe to part without resentment,
yet inside, my heart is knotted with increasing pain.
Is it not with a heavy heart that I think of you?
But the lord's gate is ninefold deep.
Fierce dogs bark loudly to meet me,
and the passes and bridges are closed and impassable.
August Heaven overflows with autumn rain;
when will the Earth ever become dry?
Alone I guard this lack of favor,
looking up at the floating clouds and sighing forever.
Why are the worldly customs so clever
as to turn their backs on the plumbline and change the rules?
They reject the Qí Jì and do not ride them,
but whip the hacks to take the road.
Does this age truly lack Qí Jì?
It is truly that no one can drive them well.
Seeing that those holding the reins are not the right people,
the horses kick and gallop far away.
Wild ducks and geese peck at grain and water-plants,
while the Phoenix soars higher and higher.
A round hole and a square peg—
I knew from the start they would mismatch and be hard to fit.
All the birds have places to perch,
yet the Phoenix alone wanders with no place to alight.
I wish to hold a gag in my mouth and remain silent,
having once been graced by your great kindness.
Tài Gōng was ninety before he became illustrious;
he truly had not met his match before then.
Where, they ask, shall the Qí Jì return?
Where, they ask, shall the Phoenix perch?
Changing antiquity and altering customs, the age declines;
the physiognomists of today only praise the fat.
The Qí Jì hide away and are not seen;
the Phoenix flies high and does not descend.
Even birds and beasts know to cherish virtue;
how can it be said that worthy men find no place to stay?
The Qí Jì do not rush forward to seek harness;
the Phoenix does not greedily or blindly eat.
You cast me aside and do not examine me;
even though I wish to be loyal, how can I?
I wish to be silent and break off all ties,
yet I secretly dare not forget the great kindness from the start.
Alone I grieve that sorrow hurts a person,
how can this pent-up gloom ever end?
Frost and dew fall miserably together,
yet the heart still hopes for a way out.
Sleet and snow increase in chaotic mixture,
and I know the encounter with my fate is about to arrive.
I wish for a lucky chance to wait,
to die in the vast wilderness among the weeds.
I wish to go and wander directly,
but the road is blocked and impassable.
I wish to follow the path and drive smoothly,
but I do not know which way to go.
Thus I am confused in the middle of the road;
I can only suppress my feelings and learn to recite.
My nature is foolish and shallow;
truly, I have not attained ease of mind.
I secretly admire the great spirit of Shēn Bāo Xū,
yet I fear the era is not stable.
Why are the worldly customs so clever
as to destroy the rules and change the patterns?
Alone I am upright and do not follow them,
wishing to follow the bequeathed teachings of the former sages.
To be illustrious in a turbid world
is not what my heart enjoys.
Rather than having a name without righteousness,
I would rather live in poverty and maintain high ideals.
I do not eat carelessly to be full,
nor do I dress improperly to be warm.
I secretly admire the legacy of the poets,
wishing to entrust my will to simple fare.
Obstructed and frustrated without end,
I drift in the vastness without limit.
Having no furs to resist the winter,
I fear a sudden death without seeing the sun of spring.
In the long nights of late autumn,
the heart is tangled and filled with grief.
Years and seasons pass by and the sun rises high,
yet I am melancholy and pity myself.
The four seasons come in turn to complete the year;
the Yin and Yang cannot be made to linger.
The bright sun sinks low and is about to set;
the bright moon is worn away and diminished.
The year passes hurriedly to its end;
old age creeps on and life becomes even more slack.
My heart is swayed by joy and daily hope,
yet I am sorrowful and without expectation.
Inwardly, I am pained by a desolate grief,
I sigh deeply and my sobbing increases.
The years flow on and days pass away,
old age is vast and empty, with nowhere to rest.
I strive diligently, hoping for progress,
yet I am hindered, staying long and hesitating.
Why do those drifting floating clouds,
so swiftly block and hide this bright moon?
My loyalty is clear and wishes to be seen,
yet it is dark and overcast, failing to reach its goal.
I wish for the bright sun to travel openly,
but the misty clouds shroud and cover it.
Secretly, I am restless in my desire to be loyal,
but some would blacken and stain me.
The lofty conduct of Yáo and Shùn
was clear even in the darkness, reaching up to heaven.
Why is there such treacherous jealousy,
covering them with the false name of being unkind?
Even the brilliance of the sun and moon
is sometimes dim and has spots.
How much more so the affairs of a state,
which are complex and tangled.
I wear a lotus garment so fine and soft,
but it is wide and loose, and cannot be belted.
Proud of my beauty and boasting of my strength,
I rely on the integrity of those around me.
They hate my sincere and refined beauty,
preferring those who are merely flamboyant.
The crowd scurries and advances daily,
while the beautiful one goes far away and travels further.
The farmer stops plowing and idles about,
fearing the fields will be overgrown with weeds.
Affairs are endless and full of selfishness,
secretly I grieve for the coming ruin and defeat.
The world follows the same pattern and shows off,
how obscure are slander and praise!
Now I adorn myself and look in the mirror,
in the future I can still go into hiding.
I wish to send a message by a shooting star,
but alas, it is so fleeting and hard to catch.
In the end, I am blocked by these floating clouds,
below it is dark and gloomy without light.
Yáo and Shùn both had those they could appoint,
so they could sleep on high pillows and be at ease.
Truly, having no resentment toward the world,
why should my heart take on such fear and trembling?
Riding a swift Qíjì steed,
what use is there for a driver to use a heavy whip?
Truly, city walls are not enough to rely on,
so even heavy armor, of what benefit is it?
I wander cautiously without end,
grieving in confusion and sorrowful constraint.
Life in this world is like a passing moment,
yet my deeds are unfinished and without result.
I wish to stay hidden and unseen,
yet I still desire to spread my name throughout the world.
But I drift aimlessly and meet no one,
I am simply foolish and bring suffering on myself.
The vastness is boundless and infinite,
where can I suddenly soar and alight?
The state has a fine steed but knows not how to ride it,
why search so frantically for another?
Níng Qī sang beneath his cart,
Huán Gōng heard him and recognized his worth.
Without a Bó Lè who is good at judging horses,
who now can make others praise it?
I weep without ceasing while I think,
only by focusing my intent can I achieve it.
Many are the pure-hearted who wish to be loyal,
but jealousy spreads and blocks them.
I wish to leave my unworthy body and depart,
setting my wandering will free among the clouds.
Riding the concentrated pure essence,
racing with the profound and deep gods.
Using the white rainbow as a side-horse, fluttering,
passing through the abundant throng of spirits.
To the left, the Zhū Què soars,
to the right, the Cāng Lóng gambols.
Summoning the Lord of Thunder with a rumbling sound,
calling Fēi Lián who speeds along.
In front, the chariots clank and ring,
behind, the supply wagons follow in order.
Carrying cloud-banners that wave and curl,
escorted by a great host of cavalry.
My plan is firm and cannot be changed,
I wish to carry it out until it is good.
Relying on the great virtue of Sovereign Heaven,
I return while my lord is still unharmed.
Since my youth, I have been pure and incorruptible,
I have practiced righteousness without ceasing.
Holding fast to this great virtue,
I am dragged down by common customs and become defiled.
Above, there is no way to examine this great virtue,
so I long suffer disaster and sorrow.
The Sovereign said to Wū Yáng:
"There is someone below, and I wish to help him.
His soul and spirit are scattered; use divination to find them and give them back!"
Wū Yáng replied:
"I am in charge of dreams. The Sovereign on High is hard to obey.
If I must divine and give them back,
I fear that later he will decline,
and will no longer have use for Wū Yáng."
Then he went down and summoned:
O soul, come back! You have left your constant body;
why do you go to the four quarters?
Leave your place of joy
and encounter those ill omens!
O soul, come back!
In the East, you cannot find shelter.
There are giants a thousand fathoms tall, who seek only souls.
Ten suns come out in turn, melting metal and dissolving stone.
They are all used to it, but if a soul goes there, it will surely be dissolved.
Come back! You cannot find shelter there.
O soul, come back!
In the South, you cannot stay.
Tattooed foreheads and black teeth;
they get human flesh for sacrifice
and make mincemeat of the bones.
Vipers are thick there, and giant foxes roam for a thousand miles.
The great nine-headed serpent darts back and forth,
swallowing men to nourish its heart.
Come back!
You cannot tarry there long.
O soul, come back! In the West are dangers,
moving sands for a thousand miles.
You would be whirled into the Abyss of Thunder,
smashed to pieces and unable to stop.
If by chance you escape, outside is a vast wilderness.
Red ants as big as elephants, black wasps as big as gourds.
The five grains do not grow there,
they eat only clumps of weeds.
The ground there rots a man's flesh,
and if you seek water, none can be found.
You would wander with nothing to lean on,
in a vastness that has no end.
Come back! I fear you will bring harm upon yourself.
O soul, come back!
In the North, you cannot stay.
Heaped ice towers high,
and snow flies for a thousand miles.
Come back!
You cannot stay there long.
O soul, come back! Do not go up to heaven.
Tigers and leopards guard the nine gates, snapping at and harming people from below.
There is a giant with nine heads, who can uproot nine thousand trees.
Jackals and wolves with vertical eyes roam in packs;
they hang people up for sport and cast them into deep abysses.
Only after reporting to the Sovereign can one close one's eyes in sleep.
Come back! Going there, I fear you will endanger your person.
O soul, come back!
Do not go down to this Yōu Dū.
Tǔ Bó has nine coils,
his horns are sharp and menacing.
With thick back and bloody thumbs,
he chases people at a gallop.
Three eyes and a tiger's head,
his body is like that of a bull.
These all find human flesh sweet;
come back!
I fear you will bring disaster on yourself.
O soul, come back! Enter the gate of Xiū Mén.
The skilled invoker summons you, walking backward to lead the way.
Baskets from Qín, silken threads from Qí, and nets from Zhèng.
The ritual implements are all prepared; I give a long cry and call out.
O soul, come back! Return to your old home.
In heaven and earth and the four quarters, there are many thieves and villains.
An image is set in your chamber; it is quiet, peaceful, and secure.
The high hall and deep rooms have balustrades and tiered porches.
Tiered terraces and stacked pavilions look out over high mountains.
Lattice doors with red hangings and carved patterns linked together.
In winter there are cozy inner rooms, and in summer the rooms are cool.
Streams and valleys wind and turn, with water flowing and murmuring.
A bright wind stirs the huì grass and floods the noble orchids.
Passing through the hall into the inner room, with red dust-mats.
The polished rooms are adorned with kingfisher feathers and hung with curved jades.
Kingfisher and pearl-covered quilts shine with a uniform brilliance.
Fine mats and hangings brush the walls, and silk bed-curtains are spread.
Embroidered bands of patterned silk are tied with precious jade ornaments.
The sights within the room are many, full of rare and strange things.
Orchid-scented oil and bright candles, all the beautiful countenances are prepared.
Twice eight maidens attend you at night, taking turns in succession.
The virtuous daughters of the Nine Marquises, many and surpassing the common crowd.
Their thick hair is styled in different ways, filling the palace.
Their looks and manners are beautifully matched, following you through the ages.
With delicate faces and firm characters, they are truly full of feeling.
Beautiful faces and elegant forms fill the inner chambers.
Moth-eyebrows and long, sweeping eyes flash with light.
With delicate skin and fine textures, they cast lingering, soulful glances.
In detached pavilions and long-curtained halls, they wait for the lord’s leisure.
Curtains of kingfisher feathers and canopies of emerald silk adorn the high hall.
Red walls and vermilion panels, with rafters of dark jade.
Looking up at the carved beams, painted with dragons and snakes.
Sitting in the hall or leaning on the balustrade, overlooking the winding pond.
Lotuses begin to bloom, mixed with water-caltrop and lily.
Purple stems like screens, their patterns rippling like waves.
Banners with leopard skin patterns line the sloping banks.
Chariots and carriages have halted; infantry and cavalry stand in rank.
Orchids grow by the doors, and fences are made of jade-like wood.
O soul, come back! Why wander so far?
Your family is all assembled; the food is diverse and plentiful.
Rice, glutinous millet, and early wheat are mixed with yellow grain.
Bitter, salty, and sour flavors; pungent and sweet are all provided.
Tendons of fat oxen, stewed until tender and fragrant.
Blending sour and bitter tastes, the soups of *Wú* are served.
Stewed turtle and roasted lamb, served with cane juice.
Boiled swan and braised duck, fried wild geese and cranes.
Steamed chicken and turtle stew, sharp and savory without being cloying.
Fried cakes and honeyed sweets, with malt sugar treats.
Jade-like wine and honey drinks fill the winged cups.
Straining the dregs and drinking it chilled, the ale is clear and cool.
Beautiful vessels are set out, filled with jade-like nectar.
Return to your old home, where you are honored and safe.
Before the dishes are cleared, the female musicians are lined up.
They set up the bells and strike the drums, performing new songs.
*Shèjiāng* and *Cǎilíng*,
followed by the performance of *Yánghé*.
The beauties are now tipsy, their faces flushed vermilion.
With playful looks and distant gazes, their eyes are like surging waves.
Clad in patterned silks and fine fabrics, they are elegant but not gaudy.
Long hair and trailing tresses, their beauty is dazzling and manifold.
Two groups of eight in perfect form
perform the dances of *Zhèng*.
Their sleeves cross like poles,
then they lower themselves toward the mats.
Flutes and zithers join in a wild chorus,
while the resonant drums are struck.
The palace court vibrates and shakes
with the performance of *Jīchǔ*.
Songs of *Wú* and chants of *Cài*
are played in the mode of *Dàlǚ*.
Men and women sit together, mingling without restraint.
Silk belts and hat-strings are loosened, tangled in confusion.
The alluring beauties of *Zhèng* and *Wèi* come and are presented together.
The final notes of *Jīchǔ* are the most outstanding.
Bamboo pieces and ivory dice for the game of *Liùbó*.
Divided into sides, they advance together, pressing each other hard.
Rolling the "owl" to win the stakes, they shout for the "five whites."
Using dice of *Jìn* manufacture and rhinoceros-horn pieces, they pass the bright day.
Clanging bells on their stands, plucking the zithers of catalpa wood.
The joy of wine does not cease, continuing through day and night.
Orchid-scented oil in bright candles, with ornate lamps set about.
They weave together their deepest thoughts, and the fragrance of orchids spreads.
People reach their limits of joy, composing verses with one heart.
Drinking ale to the fullest delight, enjoying the company of kin and old friends.
O soul, come back! Return to your old dwelling.
The Envoi says:
At the start of the year in early spring, I went on my journey south.
The green duckweed has leaves of equal size, and the white angelica grows.
The road passes through *Lújiāng*, to the left of the long marsh.
Leaning over the ponds and fields, I gaze far across the expanse.
Dark horses harnessed in fours, a line of a thousand chariots.
Hanging torches spread their light, their heat rising to the dark sky.
Moving fast or slow at times, the leaders race ahead.
Restraining the horses as if to stop, then guiding the chariots to turn back right.
Competing with the King at *Mèng*, testing who is first or last.
The King personally shoots his arrows, fearing the blue rhinoceros.
The bright sun follows the night; time cannot be stayed.
Orchids cover the paths, and the road becomes overgrown.
Deep and wide are the waters of the *Jiāng*, with maple trees upon the banks.
Looking as far as the eye can see for a thousand miles, my heart is grieved by the spring.
O soul, come back! Lament for *Jiāngnán*!
The green spring has received its turn, and the bright sun shines.
The breath of spring bursts forth, and all things hurry into life.
Though darkness and cold spread through the ways, the soul has no escape.
Soul and spirit, come back! Do not wander far away.
O soul, come back!
Do not go east or west,
nor to the south or north.
To the east is the great sea,
where the drowning waters flow on and on.
Hornless dragons swim together,
floating up and down endlessly.
Mist and rain fall incessantly,
white and vast in a thick expanse.
O soul, do not go east!
The *Tāng* Valley is desolate and silent.
O soul, do not go south!
To the south is a blazing fire for a thousand miles,
where vipers slither.
The mountain forests are steep and narrow,
where tigers and leopards roam.
There are *yúyóng* fish and "short-fox" monsters,
and the great python rears its head.
O soul, do not go south!
The sand-spitters will wound your body.
O soul, do not go west!
To the west are the drifting sands,
stretching out vast and wide.
There are creatures with swine-heads and vertical eyes,
with disheveled and shaggy hair.
Long claws and serrated teeth,
they break into wild and mocking laughter.
O soul, do not go west!
There are many things to harm and wound you.
O soul, do not go north!
To the north is the Cold Mountain, where the *Zhuólóng* dragon glows red.
The waters of *Dài* cannot be crossed,
they are deep beyond measure.
The sky is white and vast, the cold is frozen and congealed.
O soul, do not go there! The North Pole is full of peril.
Soul and spirit, come back! To a place of leisure and quiet.
Indulge yourself in *Jīngchǔ*, where you will be safe and settled.
Satisfy your will and exhaust your desires, your heart will be at peace.
Joy for your whole person forever, your years and life extended.
O soul, come back! The joy is beyond words.
The five grains are piled high, and wild rice is prepared.
Cauldrons of stewed meat fill the sight, seasoned to a perfect fragrance.
Quail, pigeons, and swans are served, with the flavor of wolf-meat soup.
O soul, come back! Taste whatever you desire.
Fresh turtle and sweet chicken, served with the curd of *Chǔ*.
Minced pork and bitter dog-meat, with sliced herbs and water-mats.
Sour dishes of *Wú* with wormwood and southernwood, not thin or watery.
O soul, come back! Choose whatever you please.
Roasted crows and steamed ducks, with braised quails laid out.
Fried crucian carp and stewed sparrows, the savory flavor remains.
O soul, come back! Fine foods are presented first.
Four kinds of ale are all ripe, not harsh to the throat.
Clear and fragrant, drunk chilled, they do not lead to weary stupor.
Sweet wine of *Wú* made with white yeast, mixed with the juices of *Chǔ*.
O soul, come back! Do not be anxious or afraid.
Musicians from *Dài*, *Qín*, *Zhèng*, and *Wèi*
play the sounding flutes and pipes.
They perform the *Jiàbiàn* of *Fúxì*,
and the *Láoshāng* of *Chǔ*.
Singing in harmony with *Yáng’ā*, while the flutes of *Zhào* lead the way.
O soul, come back! Settle in your home of *Kōngsāng*.
Two groups of eight join in the dance, presenting poems and rhapsodies.
Striking bells and tuning chimes, the revelry delights the people.
Four singers compete in vigor, exhausting every variation of sound.
O soul, come back! Listen to the songs and compositions.
Vermilion lips and pearly teeth, graceful and beautiful.
Matchless in virtue and fond of leisure, they are practiced and elegant.
Full in flesh and delicate in bone, they are well-proportioned and pleasing.
O soul, come back! Be at peace and ease.
With beautiful eyes and fitting smiles,
their moth-eyebrows are long.
Their appearance is refined and elegant,
with youthful, rosy faces.
O soul, come back!
Be quiet and at peace.
Grand and tall, ample and vast,
beautiful and fine.
Full cheeks and well-set ears, curved eyebrows like a compass.
With generous hearts and gentle manners, their beauty is displayed.
Slender waists and elegant necks, like the style of *Xiānbēi*.
O soul, come back! Let your thoughts of resentment fade.
With easy tempers and sharp minds, they carry out their duties.
Using white powder and black brow-paint, they apply fragrant oils.
Long sleeves brush the face, well-skilled in detaining guests.
O soul, come back! To enjoy the evenings.
With black hair and straight eyebrows, their beautiful eyes are soft.
Dimples in their cheeks and fine teeth, their laughter is charming.
Full in flesh and delicate in bone, their bodies are lithe and graceful.
O soul, come back! Indulge in whatever is convenient.
The great halls are vast and wide, the vermilion rooms are fine.
In the southern chamber is a small terrace, looking out where the eaves-drops cease.
Winding rooms and covered walkways, suitable for keeping pets.
Riding in chariots or walking for pleasure, hunting in the spring parks.
Jade hubs and decorated crossbars, their splendor is magnificent.
Angelica, orchids, and cinnamon trees, their fragrance fills the paths.
O soul, come back! Let your thoughts be free.
Peacocks fill the garden, and phoenixes are kept there.
Large cranes and wild geese gather at dawn, mixed with herons and cranes.
Swans and egrets fly in turn, with the long-tailed *sùshuāng*.
O soul, come back! Where the phoenixes soar.
With smooth skin and joyful faces, your vital energy is robust.
May your body always be well, and your long life be preserved.
Your family fills the court, with ranks and stipends in abundance.
O soul, come back! Your dwelling place is fixed.
The paths stretch for a thousand miles, the people come forth like clouds.
Noble lords with triple scepters, their listening is like that of spirits.
Observing the unfortunate and the hidden, the orphaned and widowed are cared for.
O soul, come back! Rectify your descendants.
Fields and towns in a thousand plots, the people are numerous and prosperous.
Your beauty covers all the streams, your virtue and grace are manifest.
First with majesty and then with culture, goodness and beauty are clear.
O soul, come back! Rewards and punishments are justly applied.
Your fame is like the sun, shining upon the four seas.
Your virtuous reputation matches Heaven, and the myriad people are well-governed.
To the north it reaches Yōulíng, and to the south it reaches Jiāozhǐ.
To the west it borders Yángcháng, and to the east it reaches the limit of the sea.
O soul, come back! Honor the worthy scholars.
Promulgate policies and promote righteous conduct; forbid cruelty and violence.
Raise the eminent to fill the palace steps; punish the mocking and dismiss the weary.
The upright and exceptional occupy their positions, near the banner of Yǔ.
Heroes and elites administer the government, and flowing grace is bestowed.
O soul, come back! It is for the sake of the state.
Mighty and majestic, the virtue of Heaven is bright.
The Sāngōng are solemn and dignified, ascending and descending the hall.
The Zhūhóu all arrive in full, and the Jiǔqīng are established.
The bright target center is set, and the Dàhóu is spread out.
Holding bows and grasping arrows, they bow and yield to one another.
O soul, come back! Follow the ways of the Sānwáng.
